<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
For every $N\ge9$, starting from $2$ with the cycle $+,\times,-,\div$, all of
$1,\dots,N$ can be made in exactly $N-1$ moves, and no fewer is possible.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:lower}
If $s\in\{1,\dots,N\}$, then making all of $1,\dots,N$ starting from $s$ takes at
least $N-1$ moves.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We start with $1$ number (the number $s$), so $N-1$ numbers are missing from
$\{1,\dots,N\}$. Since each move creates at most $1$ new number, reaching $N$
numbers requires at least $N-1$ moves.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A sequence of moves is \emph{perfect} if it makes all of $1,\dots,N$ in exactly
$N-1$ moves. In a perfect sequence, every single move must make a previously
unconstructed number between $1$ and $N$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
For $P=10$ ($q=2$) we have $H=15$ and $3P=30$. Starting after the base sequence
for $10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:base}), the tripling step is shown in
Table~\ref{tab:ex10}. Each number that a later division halves is printed in bold
colour where it is made and where it is halved. Together, the moves make
$11,\dots,30$, each once.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:tripling}
If $P\equiv2\pmod4$, $P\ge10$, and $P$ has a perfect sequence from $2$, then so
does $3P$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The $2P$ new moves follow the $\mathrm{AMSD}$ cycle. Every operand is either in
$\{1,\dots,P\}$ or was made earlier, and every division is exact. Moves
$\mathrm{M},\mathrm{S},\mathrm{A}$ generate $Y$ and moves $\mathrm{D}$ generate $X$, each number once.
So after $(P-1)+2P=3P-1$ moves, we have constructed all of $\{1,\dots,3P\}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Extend a completed interval $\{1,\dots,P\}$ to $3P+2$, where $P=4q+2$, $H=6q+3$ and
$T=3P=12q+6$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:allP}
Every $P\ge10$ with $P\equiv2\pmod4$ has a perfect sequence from $2$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By induction on $q$, where $P=4q+2$. For $q\le6$, $P$ is one of the base cases in
Appendix~\ref{app:base}. For $q\ge7$, write $q=3r+a$ with $a\in\{1,2,3\}$ and
$2\le r<q$. By induction, $P'=4r+2$ has a perfect sequence, and
$P=3P'+4(a-1)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:tripling} or the patch for $c=4$ or $c=8$ completes
the step. Soundness of every patch is proved in Appendix~\ref{app:proof}
(Lemma~\ref{lem:patches}).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:large}
Every $N\ge34$ has a perfect sequence from $2$ with the cycle $\mathrm{AMSD}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $c$ be the offset for $N\bmod12$ from Table~\ref{tab:offsets}, and let
$P=(N-c)/3$. Then $P\equiv2\pmod4$ and $P\ge10$ (with $P\ge14$ when $c=1$).
Lemma~\ref{lem:allP} gives a perfect sequence for $P$. If $c=0$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:tripling} extends it to $3P=N$. Otherwise, Lemma~\ref{lem:patches}
in Appendix~\ref{app:proof} shows that applying patch $c$ yields a perfect sequence
for $3P+c=N$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:lower} shows that at least $N-1$ moves are needed. For $N\ge34$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:large} gives a perfect sequence. For $9\le N\le33$, a perfect
sequence is given in Section~\ref{sec:lower} ($N=9$), Appendix~\ref{app:base}
($N=10,14,18,22,26$), Lemma~\ref{lem:tripling} and Lemma~\ref{lem:patches} with
$P=10$ ($N=30,32$), or Appendix~\ref{app:small} (all other $N$).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:patches}
Let $P=4q+2$, and let either $c\in\{2,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,15\}$ and $q\ge2$, or $c=1$
and $q\ge3$. If $P$ has a perfect sequence from $2$, then the tripling construction
for $P$, with its final round (or final two rounds) replaced by the patch for $c$, is
a perfect sequence for $3P+c$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $d\in\{1,2\}$ be the number of rounds the patch deletes, and let $R$ be the set
of numbers those rounds made (the removed numbers).

The final round of the tripling construction is $j=P/2-1=2q$. Its multiplication
gives $C_{2q}=3(P-2q)=6q+6=H+3$, so its subtraction and addition give $H+2$ and
$H+4$, and its division gives $H-2q=4q+3=P+1$. Since $2q\ge4$, this is not one of the
swapped rounds $1$ and $2$. In the same way, round $2q-1$, which is at least $3$,
makes $H+6$, $H+5$, $H+7$ and $H-(2q-1)=P+2$. Hence
\begin{align*}
  R&=\{P+1,\,H+2,\,H+3,\,H+4\} && (d=1),\\
  R&=\{P+1,\,P+2,\,H+2,\dots,H+7\} && (d=2).
\end{align*}
Tripling makes each number of $\{1,\dots,3P\}$ exactly once, and the deleted rounds
are the last ones, so no kept move uses a number from $R$. When the patch starts,
the numbers available are therefore exactly
\[
  K=\{1,\dots,3P\}\setminus R.
\]
A round begins on $\mathrm{M}$, so the patch also begins on $\mathrm{M}$.

\paragraph{}
Each table lists its operations in the order $\mathrm{M},\mathrm{S},\mathrm{D},\mathrm{A},\mathrm{M},\dots$.
Expanding each calculation in terms of $q$ gives the stated result, for example
$3\times(2q+2)=6q+6=H+3$ and $4\times(3q+2)=12q+8=T+2$. These are identities, so they
hold for every $q$.

\paragraph{}
Every division is by $2$, and every numerator is one of $8q+6$, $8q+8$ or $T+2i$ with
$2\le i\le7$. All of these are even for every $q$, since $T=12q+6$ is even.

\paragraph{}
The Result column of each patch lists the numbers of $R$ together with
$T+1,\dots,T+c$, each once. For $q\ge1$ these are all different, since
\[
  P+2=4q+4<6q+5=H+2\qquad\text{and}\qquad H+7=6q+10<12q+7=T+1.
\]
None of them is available before it is made, because the numbers of $R$ were deleted
and $T+i>3P$. So every move makes a new number of $\{1,\dots,3P+c\}$.

\paragraph{}
An operand marked \emph{line $i$} is made earlier in the same patch. The other
operands are of two kinds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
  \item \emph{Blank entries}, where both operands must lie in $\{1,\dots,P\}$. Apart
    from the constants $2,3,4$ and $6$, these operands are $2q+2$, $2q+3$, $3q+2$,
    $3q+4$ and $3q+5$. The first four are at most $4q+2=P$ when $q\ge2$. The last
    satisfies $3q+5\le P$ only when $q\ge3$, and it appears only in line~9 of the
    patch for $c=1$. This is why that patch needs $P\ge14$.
  \item \emph{Kept entries}, where each operand must lie in $K$. Apart from the
    constants $1$ to $4$, the kept operands are
    \[
      H+1,\quad H+5,\quad H+8,\quad P+3,\quad P+5,\quad 8q+6,\quad 8q+8,\quad T,
    \]
    where $8q+6=2P+2$ and $8q+8=2P+4$. Each is at most $3P$, so it is enough to check that none lies in $R$. Recall
    that $R\subseteq\{P+1,P+2\}\cup\{H+2,\dots,H+7\}$ and that $P+2<H$.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item $H+1$, $H+8$ and $T$ are outside both ranges.
      \item $H+5$ is used only by the one-round patches $c=4,\dots,10$, where
            $H+5\notin R$.
      \item $P+3$ and $P+5$ are above $P+2$, and below $H+2$ because $4q+7<6q+5$
            for $q\ge2$.
      \item $2P+4=H+(2q+5)$ and $2q+5\ge9$, so it is above $H+7$.
      \item $2P+2=H+(2q+3)$. For $q\ge3$ we have $2q+3\ge9$, so it is above $H+7$.
            For $q=2$ it equals $H+7$, which lies in $R$ only for the two-round
            patches $c=1$ and $c=15$. The patch for $c=1$ is used only with
            $q\ge3$, and in the patch for $c=15$ line~3 makes $H+7$ before line~23
            uses it.
    \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{}
The patch has $4d+c$ moves and makes the $4d$ numbers of $R$ together with $c$ new
ones. The whole sequence therefore has $(P-1)+2P+c=3P+c-1$ moves, and by the checks
above it makes every number of $\{1,\dots,3P+c\}$ exactly once. So it is perfect.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
